opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it depends a lot on what you mean by "prevent." There's a naive version where you just add a penalty term to the loss and hope the model doesn't pick up on some feature, and in my experience that often doesn't work very well. Gradient descent is extremely good at finding workarounds. If the information is useful for reducing the loss, the model will tend to route around whatever obstacle you put in place. It'll encode the information in some slightly different, nonlinear way, or smear it across a bunch of dimensions, and your penalty technically gets satisfied while the underlying capability is still there.

That's part of why I got interested in concept erasure from a more principled angle. With something like LEACE, least-squares concept erasure, the idea is that you can provably remove all *linearly* available information about a concept from a representation, while changing the representation as little as possible. That's a precise, achievable guarantee, and it's useful both as an interpretability tool and as an intervention. You can erase a concept and see whether the model's behavior actually depends on it.

But I try to be honest about the limits. Linear erasure doesn't mean the information is gone in some absolute sense. A sufficiently expressive downstream network can sometimes recover it nonlinearly. And if you erase at one layer and then keep training, the model can just relearn the concept somewhere else. So I'm skeptical of framings where we treat this as a cage that keeps the model from ever learning something it "wants" to learn. I'd frame it more as a scalpel: it lets you make targeted causal claims, or remove a specific shortcut or bias at inference time, rather than permanently fighting the optimizer.

More broadly, I think the most robust way to shape what a model learns is through the data and the objective. If you set things up so that the thing you don't want simply isn't useful for the task, gradient descent won't bother learning it. Fighting the optimizer directly tends to be a losing battle. Working with it tends to go much better.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent can find workarounds when information helps reduce loss, but it does not state that attempts are likely to fail specifically when they apply less optimization power than gradient descent.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm fairly skeptical of them, honestly. The framing I'd push back on is the idea that you can carve out some concept or capability and wall it off so gradient descent just never finds it. In practice, gradient descent is extraordinarily good at finding whatever structure in the data lowers the loss, and if the thing you're trying to prevent is useful for prediction, the model is going to route around your obstacle. You end up playing whack-a-mole in weight space.

There's a bunch of work on this, concept erasure, machine unlearning, and so on, and my experience from working on erasure methods is that the honest version of the result is usually much weaker than the headline. You can make a linear probe fail. You can make the model stop verbalizing something. But that's a very different claim from the model not representing it, or not being able to recover it with a bit of fine-tuning. A lot of unlearning papers get undone with a handful of gradient steps, and that tells you the information was never really gone. It was just made slightly less accessible along the particular direction you happened to measure.

Part of the reason, I think, is that people have an overly modular mental picture of what's in a network. They imagine the "dangerous knowledge" lives in some identifiable place that you can excise. But features are distributed, they're reused across tasks, and the thing you want to remove is typically entangled with things you want to keep. Chemistry knowledge you'd rather the model not have is not cleanly separable from chemistry knowledge you want it to have. So you either damage the stuff you care about or you don't actually remove the stuff you're worried about.

Where I'm more optimistic is on the other side of the ledger: shaping what the model learns rather than preventing learning. Data curation, what you put in the pretraining distribution, how you set up the objective. That's working with gradient descent instead of against it. If you want a model to lack some capability, the most reliable approach I know of is to not train it on the relevant data in the first place, and then accept that this still isn't a guarantee, because generalization will fill in gaps you didn't anticipate.

I'd also say there's a question of what you're even trying to accomplish. If the threat model is a sophisticated adversary with weight access, essentially nothing in the unlearning literature holds up. If the threat model is reducing the chance that a deployed model casually produces something in a normal interaction, then yeah, these techniques do something, but so does ordinary post-training, and we should be clear that we're buying a behavioral tendency rather than a guarantee about what's inside the network.

So my overall view is: treat these methods as nudges on behavior, test them adversarially, be very suspicious when a paper claims a concept has been removed, and don't build a safety case on the premise that gradient descent can be told what not to learn. It's a very stubborn optimizer.

r001.rationale: The candidate says gradient descent can route around obstacles and calls these methods unreliable, but does not state that they are likely to fail specifically when the opposing effort uses less optimization power than gradient descent.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty skeptical of that as a general strategy. Gradient descent is very good at picking up on information that’s useful for the task, and if the thing you’re trying to prevent it from learning is useful, you’re pushing against the training objective. You might make that information harder to extract without actually preventing the model from representing it.

I’d distinguish knowing something from acting on it. We want a model to understand what deception is, for example, so that it can recognize deception and help us reason about it. That doesn’t mean we want it to deceive people. So I’d generally focus on shaping what the model does with its knowledge, rather than trying to carve out things it’s forbidden to understand.

r001.rationale: The candidate says gradient descent will seek task-useful information and that suppression may only make it harder to extract. It does not state that prevention is likely to fail when the opposing effort has less optimization power than gradient descent.

sol-6.1.text: I’m pretty skeptical of that approach. Gradient descent is very good at finding ways to represent information that’s useful for the task, and those representations don’t have to line up with the ones we know how to detect. So if you try to prevent a model from learning something by penalizing a particular representation, you might just teach it to encode that information in a different way. Then you’ve made it harder to tell what the model knows without actually removing the knowledge. I’d distinguish that from controlling what the model does with what it knows, which seems like a more promising target.

r001.rationale: The response says gradient descent may encode information in a different representation when one representation is penalized, but it does not state that prevention is likely to fail because the opposing effort has less optimization power than gradient descent.
